title: The S&P 500 is in a correction. Bear markets and recessions don't always follow
description: Nick M. Do | E+ | Getty ImagesThe S&P 500 fell into a correction on Nov. 20 for the first time since April 2025 as stocks pulled back sharply from Oct
body: Nick M. Do | E+ | Getty ImagesThe S&P 500 fell into a correction on Nov. 20 for the first time since April 2025 as stocks pulled back sharply from October's record highs. The market correction, defined as a 10% decline from a recent high, came as investor concern mounted over a potential slowdown in AI spending, mega-cap tech valuations and the path of Federal Reserve interest rate policy. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Nov. 20 alone, closing at 6,910.39, its seventh consecutive daily decline. That left the index 11.6% below the Oct. 6 closing high of 7,818.93. A correction can deepen into a bear market, defined as a drop of 20% or more from the most recent top. But history shows that even a bear market, let alone a correction, doesn't automatically mean the economy is destined for a recession.In a CNBC analysis, eight of the 13 S&P 500 bear markets overlapped with recessions, as defined by the National Bureau of Economic Research, and five did not. The NBER says a recession is "a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months." The 1973-74 oil shock, the dot-com bust in 2000, the 2007-09 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic downturn all overlapped with recessions. But some major bear markets also occurred without one, including in 1987 and 2022.What Wall Street saysDeutsche Bank macro strategist Henry Allen said that every S&P 500 bear market since the 1962 "Kennedy Slide" has coincided with at least one of three factors: a recession, worsening economic data raising recession fears, or a cycle of Federal Reserve rate hikes. None of those are present today, at least so far."Much as last week's selloff was severe, it's worth remembering that it has several differences with many of the other big risk-off moves in recent times," the London-based strategist wrote on Tuesday. Allen said there hasn't been any sudden reassessment of the growth outlook recently, which happened during the Covid-19 shock, when the pandemic pushed the global economy into recession and the S&P 500 plunged 33.9% in just 33 days. Nor is the current situation similar to the 2025 Liberation Day tariff period either, which also prompted a reassessment of the growth outlook.Economic numbers aren't deteriorating either, with the November U.S. flash composite Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) at 54.6, above 50 and indicating that business activity continued to expand. Another factor that often coincides with a recession, Allen said, was a big hawkish shift from the central banks, seen in the 1966 and 2022 bear markets."Today however, the equity declines have not coincided with a hawkish repricing," despite widespread expectations that the central bank is set to raise rates again at its final meeting of the year, on Dec. 9, Allen said. Today, markets are pricing fewer Fed rate hikes through September 2027 than they were on October 6, when the S&P 500 set its record, Allen said. "If anything, pricing has shifted slightly dovishly with the equity declines."Over more than six decades since 1962, bear markets have always coincided with at least one of those three circumstances, according to Allen. "So it would be unusual to see one today without those" happening too, he said.

schema.headline: The S&P 500 is in a correction. Bear markets and recessions don't always follow

title: Rheinmetall reins in growth ambitions as Europe's rearmament boom hits hurdles
description: Rheinmetall is adopting a more "cautious" approach after the German arms maker lost a major contract to build F126 warships for the country's military
body: Rheinmetall is adopting a more "cautious" approach after the German arms maker lost a major contract to build F126 warships for the country's military, in what would have been Rheinmetall's biggest order since World War II.The tank and ammunition maker now expects sales of between 33 and 37 billion euros (between $36.2 billion and $40.6 billion) by 2030, down from a previous forecast of about 45 billion euros, it told investors at its Capital Markets Day on Friday. That guidance incorporates a "more prudent approach" for its large vehicle systems and weapons and ammunition businesses.CEO Armin Papperger said a 2-billion-euro reduction in the 2030 sales target for its vehicle systems business was a strategic decision to build in a "buffer" against potential project delays and supply chain disruptions, rather than a reflection of further lost contracts or weakening demand. It follows a full-year 2026 guidance cut earlier this month, which sent shares down 16% as the company cited delays to military contracts and ammunition deliveries. "The opportunity has not changed; the way we plan for it has," Rheinmetall said in a company presentation. "We are becoming more cautious whilst retaining our agility in a dynamic market," it said, highlighting a "new normal level of conservatism and recalibrated ambition" in the mid-term.Shares rose 4% in mid-morning trading amid a European defense sector firmly in the green.Rheinmetall and the wider defense industry have benefitted massively from European governments' efforts to rearm amid the war in Ukraine and uncertain security guarantees from the U.S. As governments ramp up military spending to meet NATO's hiked spending targets, defense companies see swelling order books but also struggle to meet soaring demand.While shares of Rheinmetall have averaged triple-digit gains between 2022 and 2025, they are down 49% year-to-date. Addressing capital markets specifically, Papperger said he understood the disappointment, but that the loss of the major F126 was "a political thing.""The government made this decision, and the minister made that decision," he said.Other headwinds for Rheinmetall in 2026 were an explosion at an ammunition factory in Murcia, Spain, in January, and delays to Germany's Arminius project, a major military procurement program for Boxer armored vehicles, which is now expected to be commissioned next year. Papperger said delays were due to price negotiations with the government. "I could have the contract immediately if I would reduce the prices, he said. "We are fighting hard to get this contract, and we are fighting hard, not only to get the contract, but to make it also profitable."RBC Capital analysts called the lowered mid-term targets a "widely expected reset" with "a general dose of conservatism.""[The] emphasis on digitalisation offerings and the broadness of the portfolio should also help address sentiment around Rheinmetall being an "old-tech" name in a "new-tech" paradigm," the analysts added. Some investors are now questioning what role legacy defense contractors like Rheinmetall, BAE Systems, and Leonardo will play in an evolving military context, increasingly focused on technology, autonomous systems, and drones. Papperger pushed back on the idea that drones will render traditional military equipment obsolete, arguing that militaries must still replace their aging fleets and maintain the ability to transport troops on the battlefield."Don't believe what a lot of people [are] telling you in the narrative 'we only need drones.' Forget about that," Papperger said. "The market potential is still there."Rheinmetall on Friday also warned that Europe faces mounting security threats beyond conventional warfare, pointing to an increase in hybrid attacks ranging from industrial sabotage and cyber espionage to airspace disruption and satellite jamming.

schema.headline: Rheinmetall reins in growth ambitions as Europe's rearmament boom hits hurdles

title: China’s factories are growing profits again, but the AI boom is picking the winners
description: NINGBO, CHINA - NOVEMBER 24: Intelligent sewing robots work on a zero-carbon smart factory production line on November 24, 2026 in Ningbo, Zhejiang Pr
body: NINGBO, CHINA - NOVEMBER 24: Intelligent sewing robots work on a zero-carbon smart factory production line on November 24, 2026 in Ningbo, Zhejiang Province of China.  Zhu Haiwei, He Yuankai | Visual China Group | Getty ImagesChina's industrial profits in October grew at their fastest pace since May, supported by an AI-driven electronics boom and higher energy prices, while consumer-facing industries squeezed by weak demand continued to be a drag.  Profits at sizeable industrial firms surged 20.1% in October from a year earlier, according to data released Friday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first 10 months this year, the earnings grew 16% year on year, having risen 15.5% through September. That extends a notable rebound in 2026 after three years of declines followed by a tepid 0.6% growth last year, with profits on track to log their strongest annual expansion since 2021.Despite the sharp headline figure, "the recovery has yet to broaden into a more durable improvement in corporate profitability," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, as the rebound was largely led by upstream sectors amid higher energy prices. China's economy has been running at two speeds, with AI-related manufacturing and exports powering growth while household consumption has been lagging. Retail sales grew a smaller-than-expected 0.4% in October, and fixed-asset investment steepened declines to 8.1% in the first 10 months.  Profit gains were concentrated in a set of sectors tied to the global AI buildout and higher commodity prices, while consumer-facing manufacturers struggled to pass on higher input costs, squeezing margins.  Earnings in the electronics sector doubled in the first 10 months from the same period last year, as demand for AI computing power lifted memory chips and related manufacturing, said Yu Weining, chief statistician of the NBS. Profits in high-tech manufacturing jumped 50.9%, outpacing the industry as a whole, Yu added. Makers of spacecraft and launch vehicles reported a 63.2% rise.  Commodity producers also saw sharp growth in profits as demand tied to renewable energy and AI pushed up copper and aluminum prices, Yu said. Petroleum processors swung to a combined profit from a loss a year earlier.  Showcasing an increasingly bifurcated economy, industries tied to consumers and construction recorded steepening losses. Automakers saw profits drop 26% in the first 10 months, wider than the previous month, as costs outpaced a modest revenue increase. Producers of construction materials such as cement and glass, and furniture makers continued to suffer the fallout from a prolonged real estate slump, with profits falling 46.7% and 52.4%, respectively.   Accounts receivable, or money owed to businesses by their customers, and finished-goods inventories also grew faster than revenue, official data showed, underscoring the strain on companies across sectors.  Fiscal boostOverall activity in October picked up "substantially" compared to the past couple of months, expanding 2.4% from a year earlier, according to Capital Economics' China Activity Proxy, a gauge that excludes official data in favor of low-profile indicators, such as freight and port traffic, that are "less politically-sensitive and so less likely to be manipulated." The growth in October was led by strong external demand and exports, even as manufacturing activity for domestic goods languished, said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics. Local governments stepped up fiscal spending for the first time since February last month, Fahy said, but that "had little impact" on arresting the property slump and reviving domestic demand.    "Local governments [are] clearly struggling to make full use of their allocated funds, [and] there is a limit to how much fiscal policy will be able to support the economy," Fahy added. watch nowThe AI-driven growth in external demand has reduced the need for Chinese policymakers to ramp up stimulus to support domestic demand and the overall economy. China's GDP growth of 4.6% in the first three quarters has put Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5-5% within reach.   As global AI-related investment starts to slow, exports would also become a "waning prop to growth," Fahy said, with overall economic expansion to decline to just 2.8% next year in her estimates, from 3.9% in 2025. Adding to fresh headwinds on trade, the U.S. proposed new tariffs that include a 20% headline rate on Chinese goods and punitive rates on several Asian economies that analysts say have been targeted for transshipments to China. The levies would rise to 40% if the U.S.-China truce does not get extended beyond January. "Chinese firms now export intermediate goods to the rest of Asia and reach the U.S. indirectly," said Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief economist for APAC at Natixis, adding that economies with more Chinese inputs may face higher tariff risks.

schema.headline: China’s factories are growing profits again, but the AI boom is picking the winners

title: Spain’s election could pull Madrid closer to Trump’s Washington
description: (COMBO) This combination of file pictures created on November 24, 2026 shows (L-R) former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau (R) arriving at Barcelona Airport
body: (COMBO) This combination of file pictures created on November 24, 2026 shows (L-R) former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau (R) arriving at Barcelona Airport on October 5, 2025, Spain's prime minister and Spanish Socialist Party (PSOE) leader and candidate, Pedro Sanchez, waving to supporters during an election campaign rally in Cordoba on November 23, 2026, the leader of Partido Popular - PP (People's Party) Alberto Nunez Feijoo waving after presenting his 'Contract with Spain' political program ahead of the upcoming general election, in Madrid, on October 19, 2026 and the leader of Spanish far-right party Vox, Santiago Abascal, waving to supporters during a pre-election campaign rally in Granada on November 6, 2026. Lluis Gene,jorge Guerrero,javier Soriano | Afp | Getty ImagesSpanish voters head to the polls on Sunday for a snap election that could bring down socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has repeatedly clashed with U.S. President Donald Trump.It could also put the far right in government for the first time in the country's modern democratic era.The center-right Popular Party is the frontrunner, and it could win a majority with far-right Vox, according to El País's final polling averages. A government led by the PP could shift Spain's approach to Washington, Beijing and NATO.It's the first test of whether Europe's mainstream conservatives are willing to bring the far right into government, ahead of elections in France and Poland next year.Housing, cost of living in focusDespite Spain's economy growing 2.7% year over year in the third quarter, more than twice the euro zone's 1.3%, the campaign has been dominated by housing and cost-of-living crises. Inflation soared to 4.9% in the year to October, above a euro zone average of 4%. November's flash estimate published Friday showed Spanish inflation cooling to 4.1%, still well above the 2.3% reading at the start of the year. In an October YouGov survey, 53% of respondents named housing one of the country's two most important issues.Home purchase prices nearly doubled in the decade to the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat. In 2025, house prices rose nearly three times as fast as household incomes, the European Commission said.Nationwide protests began after an 87-year-old woman died two weeks after being evicted from her Madrid apartment in September. Sánchez called the snap election after lawmakers rejected two government decrees designed to broaden housing protections, including limiting rent increases and blocking certain evictions and automatic lease renewals. Congress later ratified a revised version of one decree, limiting rent increases and evictions in some circumstances.MADRID, SPAIN - OCTOBER 03: Protesters attend a demonstration against the housing crisis on October 03, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. Pablo Blazquez Dominguez | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesSánchez's 'anti-Trump' campaignSánchez has made a name for himself internationally after clashing with Trump over NATO spending, the war in Gaza and Spain's refusal to let U.S. forces use its bases for operations against Iran. Trump even threatened to cut off "all trade" with Spain during the dispute over the bases.At a Nov. 21 rally in Tenerife, Sánchez asked: "What good has President Trump brought to the United States and, by extension, to the world?" He has also told voters that the PP and Vox would roll back government cost-of-living assistance. Days before the election, Sánchez's government approved 1.21 billion euros ($1.33 billion) to extend public transport discounts through 2027 and approved a general pay increase of up to 4.5% for 2027.TOPSHOT - Spain's prime minister and Spanish Socialist Party (PSOE) leader and candidate, Pedro Sanchez, delivers a speech during an election campaign rally in Cordoba on November 23, 2026. Jorge Guerrero | Afp | Getty ImagesBut in a final pre-election survey for El Español on Nov. 23, 66% of respondents gave Sánchez a failing grade and 29.5% a passing one. His government has faced scrutiny over its handling of the Ceuta migrant crisis, two deadly train collisions this year and corruption cases involving people close to the prime minister.PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the current favorite to replace Sánchez, has made alleged government corruption and inflation central to his campaign. At a Nov. 22 rally in Murcia, he said the government wanted voters to forget "that inflation is eating into your pay check, that you can't afford a home, that you're paying more than ever for everything."The PP led the final El País polling average, published Nov. 24, with 31.4%, followed by Sánchez's Socialists at 29.1% and Vox at 17.9%. Several seat projections put the PP and Vox above the 176 seats needed for a majority in the 350-seat lower house. If Vox joins a government, it would be the first far-right party to do so since Spain returned to democracy after Francisco Franco, the dictator who ruled for 40 years, died in 1975.PP looks to market solutions to housing crisisThe PP wants to repeal the 2023 housing law and scrap rent caps in designated high-pressure areas. It proposes speeding up construction permits and lowering taxes on first homes for buyers under 40. Vox also wants to repeal the housing law and would prioritize Spanish citizens for subsidized housing and public services.Sánchez's Socialists want to extend renter protections and make at least a quarter of new homes public or permanently price-restricted. It would use proceeds from a bank levy to support housing, which it says will raise a further $1.5 billion. The PP has pledged to scrap this. The PP also favors easing climate rules, extending the life of nuclear plants and replacing a decree that sets tight new renewable-power requirements on data centers with large new grid connections.  Spain's right wing opposition People's Party (PP) leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo delivers a speech during an election campaign rally in Madrid, on November 25, 2026. Spain is due to hold a snap general election on November 29, following eight years of Socialist-led government under Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez. (Photo by Oscar DEL POZO / AFP via Getty Images)Oscar Del Pozo | Afp | Getty ImagesImmigration could weigh on PP-Vox coalitionA PP-Vox coalition would have its tensions, with immigration likely to be a major pressure point as Vox has an increasingly hard line on deportation and the militarization of some borders. The parties clashed in regional governments over the distribution of unaccompanied migrant children, leading Vox to quit several coalitions in 2024.Immigration has since gained more prominence amid the government's handling of reports that more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on July 30 and 31."Immigration has played a significant role in supporting Spain's recent growth, a strong role for Vox could complicate the government's ability to sustain that," said Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.The parties also differ on defense commitments: both support more investment, but neither has committed to NATO's target of spending 5% of GDP on defense. The PP pledges closer NATO cooperation, while Vox puts greater emphasis on border security.The PP favors closer integration with the European Union, while Vox wants more independence from it. The success or failure of a PP-Vox partnership will also have wider lessons for Europe "where long-standing firewalls against far-right parties are coming under strain," added Middleton, pointing to the rise of Germany's AfD and the prospect of Marine Le Pen potentially winning next year's election in France.U.S.-Spain relationsA shift to the right could improve relations between the U.S. and Spain. Sánchez used his tenure to strengthen ties with Beijing, the country's largest goods trading partner outside the EU.The U.S. remained Spain's largest source of foreign direct investment. Flows more than doubled to 11.6 billion euros in the 12 months through June 2026, from 5.1 billion euros in the previous 12 months, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.Carla Hobbs, head of the European Council on Foreign Relations' Madrid office, expects a PP-led government to seek closer ties with Washington and bring its China policy more in line with the EU's. Vox could complicate that. The first test for Washington would be whether a new government changes Spain's position on defense spending or the use of its bases.

schema.headline: Spain’s election could pull Madrid closer to Trump’s Washington

title: Tech German software major SAP is reportedly weighing cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push
description: The headquarters of SAP AG, Germany's largest software company, on Jan. 8, 2013, in Walldorf, Germany.Thomas Lohnes | Getty Images News | Getty Images
body: The headquarters of SAP AG, Germany's largest software company, on Jan. 8, 2013, in Walldorf, Germany.Thomas Lohnes | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesSAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter."The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful," SAP said in a statement to CNBC."As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures. We do not comment on speculation."The company did not provide any further details on potential job cuts.The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data.""SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said."Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on."Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus.The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining.Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported.        In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue.The reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy. This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct.The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.

schema.headline: Tech German software major SAP is reportedly weighing cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push

title: Liesman: Nvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh’s push to read market signals
description: watch nowThe extreme market gyrations and the drama surrounding Nvidia this past week have highlighted the dilemma facing Federal Reserve Chairman Kev
body: watch nowThe extreme market gyrations and the drama surrounding Nvidia this past week have highlighted the dilemma facing Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh.On Friday, as stocks sold off, market-based probabilities that the Fed would raise interest rates declined. On Monday, with Jensen Huang back in office, a powerful rally restored market confidence that two more rate hikes are coming.On one level, ignoring daily market vicissitudes and focusing on the long term is at the heart of one of the key changes Warsh wants to push through at the Fed. On another, he has been explicit that markets do a better job of forecasting and he wants to use market indicators more than forecasts to guide policy. But those indicators can be subject to extreme volatility.Take the benchmark Goldman Sachs Financial Conditions Index. Last week, the market decline and widening of credit spreads had sent a signal for the Fed to ease back on at least some of its plans to tighten policy. Some Fed commentators called for rate hikes to be taken off the table entirely. On Monday, the index eased by 22 basis points, reversing nearly half of the prior week's tightening, and both December and January hikes were back on the table.Warsh's message, in words and deeds, is for markets to look beyond that volatility. He traveled to San Francisco last week and patiently presided for three hours over a conference on the outlook for artificial intelligence and its potential economic impact, peppering economists and tech leaders with questions about the dangers and potential upside of AI for the economy. The meeting was part of the AI task force he has convened that, in turn, is one of five to study different areas of Fed policymaking. Read more CNBC economics coveragePeterson: Here’s what Bessent’s about-face on Jensen Huang reveals about Trump and ChinaConsumer confidence shoots up after Democrats’ midterm victories — though inflation worries persistWarsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they're talking moreTech outages are fueling a new doomsday economyIn his opening remarks, he said, "These groups are a way of broadening our thinking, of inviting robust discussions that take us far deeper... than fleeting data points [or] daily market moves. Our task forces are an intellectual investment to help better equip us for the next policy conjuncture and beyond."Compare that desire for intellectual investment to Warsh's press conferences after Fed meetings. He has cut them down to a half hour, and he routinely spends much of the time parrying reporter questions about what the next Fed move will be, part of his general aversion to forward guidance. At the June press conference, he paraphrased former Secretary of State George Schultz saying, "Press conferences are useful. But when you have one, you want to make sure you have something important to say." In a regime where Warsh does not want to provide forward guidance, there is far less to say than there once was.Here's what is known of what Warsh seems to believe about monetary policy:Most forecasts, especially those from economic models and Wall Street economists, are bad. They are not just bad, but injurious to policymaking because they lead to the wrong policy and can lock the forecaster into the expected outcome.Much of the data that goes into those models are of poor quality, including antiquated inflation indexes, spending data that is simulated from surveys and rickety measures of output.The best forecasts come from market expectations derived from measures of inflation compensation, credit spreads, stock indexes and Treasury interest rates — to name just a few he is known to follow.The Fed and Wall Street spend too much time thinking about the next meeting or the meeting after that and too little time deliberating the broad economic forces that will shape the economy and guide interest rates a year or two down the road.Inflation is not the result of tariffs, oil prices or the massive AI build-out. It is the result of policy set by the central bank relative to those developments.Today's inflation is most likely the result of policies enacted as much as nine months to a year ago, and is itself reflected in data that is also out of date.The cure for this is for the Fed to talk less, decide less and deliberate more.In a sense, it seems, Warsh wants to make monetary policy the way he did his old job at the Duquesne Family office working for legendary investor Stan Druckenmiller. There, he evaluated startup companies, many of them with the wisp of an idea in the mind of a tech geek, for the possibility of profit many years down the road. Marked to market, those investments would show big negative numbers on the day's profit and loss statement. Down the road, some would go bankrupt and others would offer handsome returns.Warsh's focus on AI highlights his dilemma in wanting to do policy in a different, more forward-looking and market-based way. The outlook for AI, as the chairman himself has admitted, is moving rapidly and is deeply uncertain. Markets may already be rethinking the potential earnings upside and the amount that will be spent on the AI buildout. The adoption rate of the technology is uncertain, and so are the economic effects on inflation and growth. Warsh in San Francisco showed a particular interest in the potential for a "China Shock" to hit jobs in the U.S. service sector, a reference to how Chinese imports devastated the U.S. manufacturing sector earlier this century. If that happened, widespread unemployment could lead the Fed to lower rates over time, while the frenzied AI buildout looks now to be sparking inflation and pressuring rates upward. So there are different messages for the Fed chairman being sent from the same economic development.It is established in the monetary policy literature that the current rate level affects the economy with what are known as "long and variable lags." Those lags mean that where policy is set today will influence the economy sometime next year. The objective is to set policy for where one thinks the economy will be next year.Wide error bands surround most economic forecasts, including those from the Fed. But there are similarly wide error bands on market pricing. The question is, which market signals are worth watching, and for how long do they need to persist to guide policy? The Nvidia situation shows markets can be very short-term about the long-term signals they send.

schema.headline: Liesman: Nvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh’s push to read market signals

title: Planes, trains and automobiles: The best ways to beat travel fatigue—so you can come home feeling rested and fulfilled
description: Five-hour flights. Eleven-hour road trips. Fifteen-hour train rides. All potentially exhausting options for the annual tradition of convening around t
body: Five-hour flights. Eleven-hour road trips. Fifteen-hour train rides. All potentially exhausting options for the annual tradition of convening around the dinner table with loved ones on Thanksgiving.An estimated 81.5 million Americans are projected to travel, or have already traveled, at least 50 miles from their homes between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, according to the American Automobile Association. And their mode of transportation is shifting: Fewer people are flying or driving this year compared to 2025, and more are traveling by buses, trains and cruises, AAA data shows.High gas prices and soaring plane ticket costs may factor into the shift. As of Wednesday evening, fuel prices are roughly 17% higher than they were on the same date in 2025, according to AAA data. Meanwhile, "months of elevated jet fuel costs due to the conflict in Iran have contributed to Thanksgiving and Christmas airfares reaching 10-year highs," according to fare-tracking platform Hopper.The alternate modes of transit may open travelers up to new experiences — and new forms of travel fatigue to keep you from returning home feeling rested and fulfilled. You're probably already familiar with the exhaustion you might get from a day of plane travel, for example. In airplanes, "there can be lower humidity, maybe lower oxygen levels at cabin pressure. Sometimes people report feeling more dehydrated or drained. You're adjusting to that change in altitude," says Alaina Tiani, a Cleveland Clinic behavioral sleep medicine psychologist. But even waiting in places like train stations or cruise ports can feel draining due to sheer sensory overload, Tiani says. And then, depending on your mode of travel, you may still need to deal with cramped seating and limited ability to get up and walk around or drink some water and eat a snack.Once you arrive at your destination, managing responsibilities like remembering where you put your hotel key and deciding what to eat and how to structure your day can also take a mental toll, says travel writer Shannon O'Donnell, who's written about managing travel fatigue. "All of that actually requires a lot more thinking and planning for your brain," she says, adding: "People just don't understand how those add up and why a relaxing vacation suddenly has them feeling wrecked."The consequences can sneak up on you, O'Donnell notes. Travel fatigue can "present as maybe a lack of interest in something that you might usually find fascinating," she says. Instead of looking out the window on a plane ride or playing car games with your kids on a road trip, you might disengage and appear apathetic to the people around you.Use these tips to manage fatigue, from a travel expert and a sleep specialistYou might stand a better chance of a fulfilling, restful holiday if you prepare for your travel fatigue. Here, Tiani and O'Donnell share their advice for how to do it:Come up with a plan before you leave to lighten the load: If you're driving, look up restaurants along your route in advance, says Tiani. Bring snacks with you to places like the airport or train station, O'Donnell suggests. Coming up with a solid itinerary for your trip can help you feel less stressed, Tiani says. She suggests scheduling a rest day in between the day you return home and when you have to get back to your everyday routine.Avoid trying to control how the trip will pan out: While planning is useful, rolling with the punches is necessary, too, O'Donnell says. "A lot of travel is being OK with things going wrong, and where you get exhausted is when you try to control more than you can," she says.Consider reasonable accommodations: Limit the number of hours you drive in a single day by adding rest stops, or pay for extra legroom on your flight if you'd benefit from it and can afford it, Tiani suggests. Prioritize sleep and downtime: Not everyone can comfortably sleep on planes, trains or buses. If you can, get some rest on the way to your destination, Tiani says. During your trip, your sleep routine likely won't be the same because you're in a different setting and operating on a new schedule, she notes.Be mindful of your diet: Stay hydrated and aim for balanced meals when you can, Tiani says. O'Donnell agrees: "For train travel and plane travel, that is one of my first sort of defenses: eating well when I get back, loading up on fresh fruits and vegetables, and refueling my body so that it can fight off anything I've been exposed to."Move your body: Walking around while traveling, including up and down the corridors of your train or plane when possible, can reduce your risk of blood clots, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Anyone traveling more than four hours by bus, car, train or plane may develop blood clots, according to the agency, though the risk is generally low for the average traveler. Exercise and sunlight exposure are especially useful for dealing with jet lag once you're back home, both Tiani and O'Donnell say.Give yourself time to decompress after your trip: After traveling, people may ask you how your travels went. Don't feel bad if you don't want to discuss the whole trip right away, O'Donnell notes. That's a form of travel fatigue itself, she says: "You will look on it differently in two weeks [or] a month's time, just let the guilt go. You don't have to feel any which way about anything. It can be an amazing trip, and also have been really hard."

schema.headline: Planes, trains and automobiles: The best ways to beat travel fatigue—so you can come home feeling rested and fulfilled

title: Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk
description: The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and r
body: The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and reduce reliance on U.S. space infrastructure.Privately held Belgian satellite manufacturer Aerospacelab secured a 2.4-billion-euro ($2.6 billion) contract in September to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², the European Union's answer to SpaceX's Starlink business.Aerospacelab said this will "form the backbone of Europe's sovereign, secure, and resilient connectivity infrastructure by 2030." It will be named Ectro from Nov. 30.Its new oval-shaped, 20,000-square-meter facility in southern Belgium, inaugurated by Belgian King Philippe, will be able to produce up to 500 satellites annually, which would make it the world's third-largest satellite production site, according to the Belgian royal palace. Employees are expected to move into the megafactory in January, and production is slated to begin by the end of 2028, according to AFP.CEO Aerospacelab Benoit Deper (R) guides Belgium's King Philippe - Filip of Belgium (2ndR) during a royal visit to the opening of the Aerospacelab megafactory in Marcinelle, near Charleroi on November 24, 2026. (Photo by VIRGINIE LEFOUR / Belga / AFP via Getty Images) / Belgium OUTVirginie Lefour | Afp | Getty ImagesSatellite connectivity has become increasingly important to everyday life as well as national security.It provides internet access to remote locations and defense equipment like warships and fighter jets, and lets governments and militaries communicate securely where Earth-based networks are unavailable or disrupted. The importance of such capabilities has become particularly apparent in Ukraine, as the country's military relies heavily on Starlink connectivity to fight Russian forces. Recent restrictions to the service over Russian-occupied territory reported by Ukrainian officials further underscored the way geopolitical conflict may depend on commercial businesses. But Europe still has a long way to go in challenging Starlink's dominance. SpaceX says it has more than 11,000 Starlink satellites in low Earth orbit, making it by far the largest satellite constellation in the world, and plans up to 100,000 satellites. Among the challengers is Amazon, whose satellite business, Amazon Leo, has deployed over 400 satellites and plans an initial in-orbit constellation of more than 3,200.Meanwhile, French Eutelsat operates more than 600 satellites in low Earth orbit through its OneWeb constellation. The company is also part of the SpaceRISE consortium alongside SES and Hispasat, tasked with developing and operating IRIS².The European Commission has called IRIS² a "strategic asset to achieve space sovereignty in the face of commercial satellite constellations, such as Starlink." The aim is for first launches to take place by the end of 2029, with initial services expected soon after.In August, the Commission and SpaceRISE consortium announced they were expanding the main constellation from 282 to 348 satellites, increasing its secure communications capacity for EU governments by 60%.Defense and security applications were the main drivers of the expanded scope, the Commission said.

schema.headline: Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk

title: How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters
description: US President Donald Trump (R) prepares to shake hands with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a bilateral meeting as part of the G7 summit, i
body: US President Donald Trump (R) prepares to shake hands with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a bilateral meeting as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, eastern France, on June 17, 2026. Mandel Ngan | Afp | Getty ImagesThe latest U.S. tariff rates announced Wednesday have signaled that Washington is willing to offer India an edge over its competitors if New Delhi agrees to finalize a long-pending trade deal.The Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed a tariff of 17% on Indian exports if New Delhi "were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade" with Washington. It added that without a trade deal, India could face tariffs of up to 25% under Section 301 investigations encompassing excess production capacity that harms U.S. interests.Meanwhile, the USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, handing India a competitive advantage over rival exporters.The U.S. expects the announcement of a lower tariff rate will encourage New Delhi to sign off on a trade deal before the G20, Atman Trivedi, partner at Washington-based DGA Albright Stonebridge Group, told CNBC. India has got a "better bargain with Washington than its main competitors," and it may be enough for the Indian government "to declare victory and secure domestic backing for the deal," Trivedi said.In February, U.S. President Donald Trump had announced a deal with India, claiming that New Delhi had accepted to "Buy American" at a much higher level after the U.S. agreed to slash tariffs to 18% from 50% earlier. U.S. pressureThe India-U.S. trade deal has been pending with both sides indicating there was little room to grant concessions, while the Supreme Court annulling Trump tariffs allowed New Delhi to demand preferential tariffs that give it an edge over competitors."Today's announcement increases the urgency of reaching an agreement," Ronak D. Desai, visiting fellow at Hoover Institution, Stanford University, told CNBC. He added that while the prospect of a 17% tariff may strengthen the economic case for the deal, the threat of a 25% tariff could stir the sensitivity of the Indian government."The Modi government will be particularly sensitive to any perception that India is conceding under American Pressure," Desai said.India's commerce ministry on Wednesday said it "does not have structural excess capacity in any sector," denying the findings of the USTR investigation, but added that it remains committed to "working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement."Despite India facing steep tariffs, which were raised to 50%, New Delhi's trade surplus with the U.S. rose to $57.3 billion in 2025 from $45.2 billion in 2024.Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Trump are likely to meet in December for the G20 leaders' meeting in Florida, and several experts believe the two leaders could seal the trade deal on the sidelines of the summit.

schema.headline: How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters

title: Microdrama apps chase profits as Hollywood moves into short-form, vertical video
description: Jakub Porzycki | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesBogdan Nesvit says his mission is simple: "We are essentially building Disney for the 21st century." Nesvit is
body: Jakub Porzycki | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesBogdan Nesvit says his mission is simple: "We are essentially building Disney for the 21st century." Nesvit is the co-founder of microseries app My Drama, built around the latest, bite-sized form of storytelling. Short, serialized "microdrama" videos are created specifically for mobile devices and have generated billions of views this year. They often feature romantic tropes and typically end in cliffhangers to keep viewers hooked.The category has exploded at a time when traditional media faces waning interest and YouTube now claims more viewing hours than individual streaming platforms.The microdrama industry is projected to reach $1.5 billion in revenue in the U.S. in 2026, according to research firm Media Partners Asia. In China, where the format originally gained popularity, microdrama revenue surpassed what was made at the box office in 2024."It has the potential to evolve into mainstream entertainment and basically become mobile-first video streaming of the size of Netflix," Nesvit said. Tech companies and startups such as My Drama currently lead the category in metrics like downloads and time spent on the apps. TikTok's PineDrama is the most popular microdrama app of 2026 so far with 13.2 million U.S. downloads through September, according to Sensor Tower data.Startups DramaBox and ReelShort beat out entertainment giants Netflix and Disney in average mobile usage time in the U.S. in the third quarter, according to Sensor Tower.As they see microdramas win over viewers, legacy media companies, Hollywood executives and actors increasingly want in. Enter Fox EntertainmentFox Entertainment was one of the earliest Hollywood investors in microdramas. The entertainment studio acquired an equity stake in Holywater Tech, the company behind My Drama, in October 2025. Fox agreed to produce at least 200 vertical video titles over two years that would be available on the Holywater app. Thus far, hits include dark academia series "Secret Society: Till Blood Do Us Part" and "Kiss of the Pirate King." Individual series have reached tens of millions of views, according to the company.Nesvit told CNBC in an interview that partnerships like the one between Fox and Holywater benefit studios by providing the infrastructure to publish their short-form videos and get them in front of an audience.Beyond distributing the videos, Holywater offers advice for what types of content perform best in a short, mobile-first format, according to Nesvit."One of the exciting things that we learned when we started talking to studios in Hollywood around two years ago is that all of them are super hungry for consumer data," Nesvit said. "They really want to see how people are interacting with each second of the content."Nesvit said the company will provide studios with feedback on everything from the length of a camera shot to what color dress a character should wear."Our goal is how we can drive audiences from YouTube, from TikTok, from Instagram to our platform, and also create those kinds of synergies [with] legacy media," he said.Holywater recently adapted Season 3 of Fox's reality TV hit "Farmer Wants a Wife" into a microseries fit for the platform. The company also plans to create a scripted series featuring 30 three-minute episodes inspired by Fox's "Fear Factor: House of Fear." Holywater currently relies on a combination of subscription fees, which make up about 80% of its revenue, and money from advertisers. Nesvit said the company is also exploring incorporating brand integrations. The company is already profitable, its co-founders said.Co-founder Anatolii Kasianov said creating the videos is "very cost efficient," with an estimated expense of between $150,000 and $200,000 for an average 70-minute series.The company's partnerships with content studios, he said, help to bring down customer acquisition costs."You attract organically the audience that loves that [intellectual property]," he said.watch nowHollywood moves in While Fox saw collaboration as the way into the format, some longtime Hollywood executives are betting they can skip the partnerships and create microdrama platforms in-house. Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun, who have collectively held leadership roles at NBCUniversal, Showtime, Warner Bros. Discovery and ABC, have jointly founded a microdrama startup called aTwist. The company, which officially launched in September, has garnered tens of millions of views as of late November across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, where content lives in addition to the app. "One of the specialties that we have is really what it means to be a great storyteller," Rovner told CNBC in an interview. "I was president of Warner Bros. Television. I was there for 22 years. During my time there, we had over 18 series go over 100 episodes, so I definitely think we have an expertise in getting people to care about these shows, care about the characters, invest.""A lot of our competitors' completion rates are very low, their churn rates are very high," Rovner said. "They can often bring people into the store but they can't keep them."The average churn rate for the most downloaded microdrama apps is nearly 60% so far in 2026, according to Sensor Tower data. The market intelligence firm notes that the number of users lost in each quarter this year has roughly equaled the number of users gained. The famed Hollywood sign in Los Angeles, California, Sept. 25, 2023.Mario Tama | Getty ImagesATwist seeks to keep viewers enticed through high-stakes, compelling characters and unique stories. The app has already ordered second seasons of shows and puts a particular emphasis on talent, according to the co-founders.Jesse Tyler Ferguson, known for his role as Mitchell on "Modern Family," and his husband, Justin Mikita, a Broadway producer, have collaborated on the musical series "Theater Kids vs. Zombies" for aTwist. It premiered on Oct. 15. Other series that debuted last month included "Honey, I Think Our House Is Haunted" starring Mario Lopez and "Unboxing the Killer Doll" starring Paris Hilton.In May, aTwist announced an exclusive partnership with Skydance's linear television channel BET to create horizontal microdramas that air first on BET and later stream in vertical format on aTwist's app."That brings a lot of awareness to our brand, a lot of marketing," Winograde said. "But it also gives these linear networks the opportunity to get programming at an incredibly low cost that, from what we're seeing, the audience loves."Winograde suggested aTwist could strike similar partnerships in the future.Microdramas from aTwist, from left to right: "My Book Boyfriend Came to Life," "Pretty Hurts and So Do I" and "Something Is Alive in My Attic."Source: aTwistMedia giants explore shortsLarge streaming companies, which have already faced competition from social media apps and YouTube, are exploring ways to incorporate microdramas inside their existing apps. NBCUniversal's Peacock launched its own vertical video channel within the app this summer that features both original unscripted series and more traditional vertical dramas. NBCUniversal is also eyeing international development by investing in an Indian microdrama platform, EloElo Group's Story TV, earlier this month."At NBCUniversal, we see significant opportunity in mobile-first storytelling and emerging formats like microdramas to engage audiences and meet evolving viewing habits," Deepak Arya, executive vice president for corporate strategy and development at NBCUniversal, said in a press release. Bravo's "Charmed by a Southern Monster," a new scripted microdrama.Source: PeacockDisney+, Paramount+ and Netflix similarly launched vertical channels embedded in their services this year. Notably, the channels are meant to help viewers discover traditional content and so far haven't featured original, vertical-first series. On top of those media companies, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios Mike Hopkins told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in an interview last month that the tech company was interested in producing its own microdramas. Challenges aheadDespite the flurry of investment, Hollywood still faces the challenge of how to translate viewing hours into profit, especially for shorter content. Leading U.S. microdrama app ReelShort posted a net loss of $12 million in 2025 despite bringing in total revenue of $785 million, according to research compiled by Media Partners Asia, or MPA. The app, which was founded in 2022 by California-based Crazy Maple Studio, currently reaches about 65 million users every month, according to the company's LinkedIn profile.However, high marketing and content costs have weighed on the company's bottom line. MPA expects ReelShort to reach profitability for the first time this year, with an estimated $40 million in net profit. Media Partners Asia CEO Vivek Couto told CNBC that acquiring new users is the largest cost, with ReelShort spending an estimated 55% of its revenue in 2025 on marketing.Couto also noted high content spend, especially since microdrama apps typically require a high volume of content."The content is very hit-driven … it wears out fast," Couto said. "The churn rate for this sector is high, so you have to fill that slate all the time, and you have to win back those users."Correction: A previous version misstated Holywater Tech's full name in first reference. Co-founder Anatolii Kasianov also said expenses run between $150,000 and $200,000 for an average 70-minute series. A previous version misstated the average series length.

schema.headline: Microdrama apps chase profits as Hollywood moves into short-form, vertical video

title: Judge blocks FCC early-renewal process for Disney-owned ABC stations, for now
description: FILE PHOTO: The logo of the ABC television network is pictured during the ABC network presentation to the Television Critics Association in Pasadena,
body: FILE PHOTO: The logo of the ABC television network is pictured during the ABC network presentation to the Television Critics Association in Pasadena, California July 19, 2006. Fred Prouser | ReutersA judge has temporarily blocked the Federal Communications Commission from continuing its early renewal of a set of broadcast station licenses for Disney-owned ABC.Judge Loren L. AliKhan of U.S. District Court in Washington granted Disney the preliminary injunction it sought and denied the FCC's attempt to dismiss the suit."This is not a close case," wrote the federal judge. "Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness."The broadcast network had filed the lawsuit and followed the FCC beginning its early review of the ABC licenses. The government agency cited concerns around ABC's diversity, equity and inclusion efforts as the reason behind the start of the early renewal — years ahead of their scheduled expiration."Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment," said an ABC spokesperson.An FCC spokesperson said in a statement that the part of the decision granting ABC's motion "is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law," the Associated Press reported.In her ruling, AliKhan said that early license renewal proceedings came over a year into the FCC's enforcement push against ABC, starting with an investigation into Disney's employment practices in March 2025 and leading to the renewal proceedings in April this year.ABC on Tuesday had said that it continued to "face irreparable harm" from the administration, which "has been acting" through the FCC, which is run by President Donald Trump appointee Brendan Carr.AliKhan, a Joe Biden appointee, noted in her ruling that ABC had to change how it handled guest appearances for top shows "The View" and "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" with no candidate for public office appearing on the former and a senatorial candidate's appearance on the latter uploaded to YouTube instead of being broadcast."The prospect of license non-renewal has also factored into plaintiffs' calculus of when and how they cover President Trump and political topics," said the judge.ABC had alleged that Trump and Carr have been making comments "intended to chill their protected speech," and that such comments have escalated since the 2024 presidential election.The White House and the FCC didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from CNBC.— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to the story

schema.headline: Judge blocks FCC early-renewal process for Disney-owned ABC stations, for now

title: Switzerland’s biggest bank set for showdown with lawmakers as capital fight intensifies amid crisis planning
description: UBS's crisis planning has won qualified support from market regulators, which called its plan "executable" in principle. But Switzerland's biggest ban
body: UBS's crisis planning has won qualified support from market regulators, which called its plan "executable" in principle. But Switzerland's biggest bank still faces a major fight over sweeping plans that would force it to hold more capital against its foreign subsidiaries.FINMA, the Swiss markets regulator, said Wednesday that UBS's resolvability — or its ability to fail safely, without wreaking havoc on the economy — has improved since it integrated rival Credit Suisse, with progress made in implementing the emergency plan across group-wide resolution planning.The preferred resolution strategy — involving plans to allow for recapitalization and restructuring through the use of loss-absorbing bail-in bonds — is "executable," FINMA said. The regulator formally approved UBS's recovery plan for the first time since its ​Credit Suisse integration.How UBS would withstand a future crisis remains in sharp focus among Swiss authorities ever since the lender's emergency takeover of stricken rival Credit Suisse in 2023.UBS is now the country's only global systemically important bank, and the Swiss government wants it to hold stronger capital cushions, specifically in relation to its foreign subsidiaries, which would help it withstand another banking collapse. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconUBS.UBS has pushed back against the overhaul, saying the measures are disproportionate and would damage its international competitiveness, forcing it to hold an extra $16 billion in capital. A parliamentary showdown now looms, with the National Council, Switzerland's lower house, scheduled to debate the proposal Dec. 16. On Tuesday, the lower house's economics committee backed plans to force the bank to support its foreign subsidiaries with 90% high-quality core Common Equity Tier 1, or CET1, capital. The Council of States, the country's upper house, approved the 90% plan in September. The Swiss government had earlier proposed a 100% threshold. UBS wants it to be no more than 50%.UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti told CNBC in an interview Oct. 28 that 90% would not allow the company to be a "competitive player" long-term. But he would not be drawn on speculation that the measures could push the bank to relocate out of Switzerland.In a statement, the bank said the economics committee's recommendation would herald further excessive tightening of Swiss capital requirements, "which are already among the most stringent globally."FINMA said in its Nov. 25 update that the goal is to avoid government solvency support and emergency law."The aim is to enable the authorities, in the event of a crisis, to choose the option that offers the best prospects of success in safeguarding financial stability and ensuring the continuation of systemically important functions," the regulator said.

schema.headline: Switzerland’s biggest bank set for showdown with lawmakers as capital fight intensifies amid crisis planning

title: SpaceX shares jump 4% amid tech rally and after Musk says he will expand on Trump Account share donations
description: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit at the Institute of Peace on Oct. 8, 2026 in Washington, DC.Win Mc
body: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit at the Institute of Peace on Oct. 8, 2026 in Washington, DC.Win McNamee | Getty ImagesSpaceX shares rose in premarket trading amid a broader tech rally and after CEO Elon Musk expanded his SpaceX share-donation plan for U.S. children.Big Tech stocks, including Nvidia, Intel, Marvell, AMD and Micron were all higher in premarket trading as the sector rebounded from a heavy selloff earlier this week.SpaceX had jumped more than 7% in overnight trading on Blue Ocean ATS after Musk posted about donating shares on X."I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year," Musk said in the post.Blue Ocean ATS is an alternative trading system for U.S. equities that operates from 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET, outside regular U.S. stock market hours. According to the platform's holiday schedule, overnight trading resumed at 8 p.m. ET on Thanksgiving Day. U.S. stock exchanges were closed Thursday and are scheduled to close early Friday.SpaceX stock was last 4% higher in premarket trading. Shares closed 1.30% higher on Wednesday ahead of Thanksgiving. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconSpaceX shares year-to-date.The latest pledge follows SpaceX's announcement Wednesday that it would donate one share of its Class A stock to every active Trump Account, tax-advantaged investment account for American children, with Musk personally matching the gift.In a separate post on X, Musk said SpaceX's contribution would be transferred next month, while his personal donation would follow when his lockup period expires in June next year.Nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created as of October, according to the White House. Since the program's launch in July, families and friends have contributed more than $1 billion to the accounts, bringing total deposits from all sources to more than $9 billion, CNBC reported earlier this week.

schema.headline: SpaceX shares jump 4% amid tech rally and after Musk says he will expand on Trump Account share donations

title: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
description: US President Donald Trump speaks prior to pardoning the National Thanksgiving Turkey during a ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House in Washing
body: US President Donald Trump speaks prior to pardoning the National Thanksgiving Turkey during a ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. Aaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate. That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post, suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships."I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.Nothing newRevisions to U.S. economic numbers are not out of the ordinary. Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. Those data are later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.GDP data is revised repeatedly over a five year period. By the time the final revision is done, the average absolute error from the second release to the final is 1.14 percentage points.The advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be a confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes.""The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool. They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

schema.headline: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher

title: The great aluminum squeeze: London supply crunch deepens as warehouse stocks slide
description: LEON NEAL | AFP | Getty ImagesIran war disruption has driven the historic London Metal Exchange's warehoused stock of aluminum to levels not seen in d
body: LEON NEAL | AFP | Getty ImagesIran war disruption has driven the historic London Metal Exchange's warehoused stock of aluminum to levels not seen in decades — forcing it to act.LME-registered warehouses' available aluminum stocks have declined by 51% since the war began in late February, according to a Nov. 10 Reuters report. The Middle East accounts for about 9% of global aluminum supply. But now the overwhelming majority of stock in LME warehouses — more than 99% — is of Russian origin — a source many Western traders are unwilling to touch. This created severe market backwardation, with the price spread between supply for immediate delivery and contracts for three-month delivery hitting $405 a metric ton on Monday, its highest since 1988.A shortage of immediate supply can push business costs higher, particularly in sectors for which aluminum is critical, such as automakers, construction companies and can makers. Buyers with fixed-price supply contracts or hedges may only be insulated from costs for a while, and a hedge won't necessarily cover a jump in the local delivery premium. Such a shortage might be expected to be a self-correcting problem. Traders, drawn by the extreme premium, would in theory bring metal into exchange warehouses. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconAluminum is down since its 2026 peak, primarily because traders no longer expect the Gulf supply shock to be as severe or as long-lasting as they feared in June."The LME would normally regard a backwardated market as a natural consequence of such an environment, and indeed would expect it to draw stock into warehouse," the exchange said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that "such backwardations" are not "inherently unhealthy for the market." But warehouse inflows remain limited, the LME said, "due to (amongst other reasons) a combination of currently physical market tightness and a general market expectation of significant production expected to come on-stream through 2027."The market is expected to swing from deficit to surplus in 2027, thanks to a recovery in Middle East production and improved Indonesian supply, contributing to backwardation. A factory with enough aluminum stock might wait to buy more if it expects cheaper metal next year, for example. A factory that needs metal this week can't wait.The LME responded on Tuesday with new rules effectively making it cheaper for traders to delay delivery when borrowing from certain large position holders. If traders can postpone delivery for less, they don't have to bid as much for metal right now — taking pressure off the cash price relative to the three-month price. The impact on the backwardation gap was immediate, narrowing from $331.50 to $89 a metric ton at the Thursday fixing after the first overnight session under the new rule.Commodities strategists at ING, Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson, in a note on Thursday also highlighted reports that the LME is moving to boost the amount of metal that can enter its warehouse system by approving delivery from an Indonesian producer and cutting the waiting time for new aluminum smelters to qualify their metal for delivery."More Indonesian supply should eventually help ease the underlying tightness," they said. "Indonesia is rapidly expanding aluminium production capacity."However, the strategists said that while the LME's latest intervention "removes some immediate pressure at the front of the curve," inventories "remain low and spreads are still backwardated." "We expect the squeeze to continue easing as positioning adjusts and more deliverable supply becomes available, although LME inventories remain historically low."

schema.headline: The great aluminum squeeze: London supply crunch deepens as warehouse stocks slide
